note: Worked at a hometown car wash with three machines: gold tokens for the wash, silver tokens for the vacuum, real quarters for tire shine. Became his go-to analogy for needing different gas tokens per chain.
Keeps a little bitcoin on a hardware wallet in his 'metaphorical sock drawer', and has a fat-finger send story he refuses to finish.
Admitted Jules's 'one slot that takes whatever's in your pocket' analogy works; Jules demanded she 'write it down, date it.'

Spent a summer at a bait shop run by Dale, who posted a sign bragging about throwing out a hundred dead minnows the same week five hundred new ones arrived. 'Getting Dale'd' is now Jules's phrase for falling for burn-style marketing.

Her one-number rule for any deflation claim: 'burned minus emitted.' She also admitted a second Jules analogy works (Dale handing minnows to his regulars as buy-and-distribute), and Jules again made her 'date it.'

At fifteen ran 'the corn route': bought sweet corn at a farm stand for a dollar a dozen, sold it at the lake for three, but his uncle's gas-guzzling truck (charged both ways) and corn wilting in the sun left him with about four dollars for the summer. Now his go-to picture of fees, gas and slippage.
His braai rule for margin of safety: you don't throw the steak on the second the fire's lit, you wait for proper coals, because something always goes wrong.
Admitted a third Jules analogy works (the uncle's truck making five trips = splitting trades multiplies fixed costs); Jules says it's 'already dated, in pen.'

At sixteen the only direct bus to the state fair was 'the Tuesday bus', which broke down every other week, so he took a feed-store truck, a Greyhound and his buddy's cousin's moped instead. He once got stranded at the Greyhound station with a funnel cake coupon and no fair. Now his picture of a direct route through a thin pool vs. a multi-hop route.
Admitted a fourth Jules analogy works (the Tuesday bus = an illiquid direct route losing to three efficient legs), and dated it on air.

Frames routing as a relay race: every protocol is a 'starter, middle or anchor', and a failed hop is 'the dropped baton'. Says he's stealing Jules's 'carry the actual baton, not a photo of a baton' line for pitch meetings.

His door-to-door knife summer paid partly in 'Gold Star Points'; the toaster oven he saved for went from 500 to 2,000 points as the company kept printing them, and he ended up with a cutting board. Now his picture of emissions-funded yield.
Old Walt at the hometown marina sharpened knives for a dollar a blade, cash only, and 'barely had a phone'. Jules's picture of fee-backed yield: 'nobody ever printed more Walt dollars.'
After admitting a fifth Jules analogy works, she stopped 'dating' them and now keeps a spreadsheet of his analogies that hold up.

Mr. Halvorsen kept an ice-thickness chalkboard by the hometown gas station coffee (four inches to walk, eight for a snowmobile, twelve for a pickup). Jules's cousin Derek checked once in January, drove his pickup onto March ice, went through to the front wheels, and got winched out for a tow fee. He's now 'Derek who drove on March ice', Jules's picture of passive monitoring and soft liquidation.
Her spreadsheet of Jules analogies that hold up has exactly one column, 'Held up'. Derek and the March ice is entry number six.
His braai rule for pre-commitment: decide when the steak comes off before you light the fire, not when six uncles are shouting opinions at you.

At seventeen worked Bev's Boom Barn, a fireworks tent off Highway 9 with a fire extinguisher named Gerald. Made $800 on July 3rd, multiplied it by 365, told his mom he might skip school, then sold one box of sparklers (to Bev) on July 5th. Now his picture of annualizing a 24-hour snapshot; Gerald is his picture of low utilization.
The fireworks tent is entry number seven in her 'Held up' spreadsheet of Jules analogies.

New lines: 'Big braai, lots of uncles' (more LPs at the grill means a thinner slice each), and 'you don't print a striker's season stats off one hat trick' for judging returns on 7 and 30 days, not one day.

At nineteen he delivered pizzas for Sal's one winter. His county had two Elm Streets (one in town, one out in Pine Hollow); he took an order for 412 Elm to the wrong one and ate the pizza in the truck. 'Perfect address, wrong town' is now his picture of sending tokens on the wrong network.
Sal's pizza and the two Elm Streets is entry number eight in her 'Held up' spreadsheet of Jules analogies.
His picture of running out of gas tokens: 'a delivery truck full of hot pizzas and an empty tank.'
